vignette:
Leila had worked for nearly three decades as a prison guard, a role she had carried with the same stiff reliability that had once made her proud. At 68, married and close to retirement, she had expected the institution to feel familiar and controlled. Instead, the assault that brought her to treatment left her feeling as though the ground beneath her had changed shape. It happened on a late evening shift in a corridor near the dayroom, when a male inmate she had been redirecting suddenly lunged at her, shoving her hard against the wall and striking her before colleagues pulled him off. The fluorescent lights, the abrupt silence after the shouting, and the narrow institutional hallway have remained vivid to her ever since. In the days that followed, Leila found herself replaying the scene with a harshness that was more accusation than memory. She was certain she should have protected the other staff member who had been nearby, certain she had failed in a basic duty of vigilance, and that conviction settled into the broader belief that she was no longer the capable woman she had been. Because she had come to see herself as unreliable and the world as the kind of place where an instant of inattention could get someone hurt, she began staying close to other officers, filling every gap in the day with company, and handing off the more exposed parts of her route whenever she could. Those habits made sense to her as the only responsible way to prevent another mistake, even as they quietly narrowed the life she was willing to lead. She began to think of herself as permanently on the outside now, someone who did not quite belong among people who could still trust the world to behave predictably, and she spoke with bitterness about how people could not be trusted.

Those beliefs shaped the months that followed. Leila started keeping herself constantly surrounded by people, joining coworkers in the break room, lingering after shifts, and filling evenings with visits to her adult children and neighbors, because being alone left her face to face with the attack and with her own self-reproach. The more she built her days around these safety habits, the more their usefulness seemed to prove itself, and the more she concluded that she could not cope without them. Each time she needed company to get through an evening or asked someone else to cover a task she used to manage, it felt like another small piece of evidence that she was fragile, not the capable guard she had once believed herself to be. She also began dropping responsibilities she had once managed without hesitation, asking others to cover parts of her route or avoiding tasks that would put her in less supervised corners of the prison. The more she pulled back from those duties, the more she noticed how little confidence she had in herself, and the more convinced she became that she had indeed failed to protect others when it mattered. What she had once experienced as caution hardened into a sense that she was weak and no longer fit for the role she had lived by; in turn, that shame pushed her back toward other people and away from solitary moments where the accusations grew loudest.

Her body, however, did not obey her plans to stay busy. Leila described a constant scanning of her surroundings, even in ordinary places like the grocery store and the prison parking lot, her eyes moving automatically to exits, hands, pockets, and faces. Feeling this on-edge all the time, she had gradually taken her own fear as proof that she really was no longer the steady woman she had once been. The threat she kept sensing in hallways, doorways, and sudden silences quietly confirmed the self-accusation that she was weak and could not trust herself to stay calm or competent. She said her body reacted to danger before she had time to think: shoulders tightening, heart racing, stomach dropping when a voice rose behind her or a door slammed somewhere out of sight. Unusual silence frightened her almost as much as noise. In the prison break area, if conversation stopped suddenly or a corridor went quiet, she felt something dangerous was about to happen, and she would find herself looking up and around before she knew what she was looking for. Those bodily alarms reinforced the impression that she had to stay on guard, and staying on guard meant staying with people, staying busy, and never allowing herself to drift. Yet the more she lived this way, the more she came to read her own constant vigilance as proof that the world really was unsafe and that she was right not to trust anyone. She noticed every stare, every closed door, every moment of quiet as confirmation that danger was near and that she had been foolish to think she could ever relax.

Sleep became another casualty. Leila had trouble falling asleep and often woke in the middle of the night with her body already tense, as if it had been waiting for something. On those nights she would get up, move through the house, and call a sister or sit with the television on low volume simply to avoid the silence. The lack of sleep made the next day feel thinner and more exposed, and she became even more reliant on company, more willing to hand off tasks, and more convinced that she could not afford to let her guard down. At home her husband noticed that she avoided quiet rooms and kept doors open; at work she was less willing to take the lead on rounds, preferring to stay near other officers. What frightened her most was not only the memory of the assault but the feeling that her own body had taken over the job of warning her, making her certain that danger was always about to break through. By the time she sought help, Leila was exhausted by the effort of never being alone, ashamed of how much she had stepped back, and frightened that if she did not learn how to sleep and stop scanning every silence, she would spend the rest of her life waiting for another attack.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs and shame, but it does not clearly state that these appraisals drive the avoidance, clinging to company, or task-dropping behaviors in a causal way within the same paragraph.

The vignette shows a persistent sense of danger and hypervigilance, but it does not clearly state that this threat perception causes the negative beliefs or self-accusations in a same-paragraph causal chain.

The vignette shows avoidance, staying busy, and seeking company, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies lead to the self-blaming or mistrustful appraisals in a same-paragraph causal chain.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows negative beliefs and shame, but it does not clearly state that these appraisals drive the avoidance, clinging to company, or task-dropping behaviors in a causal way within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows a persistent sense of danger and hypervigilance, but it does not clearly state that this threat perception causes the negative beliefs or self-accusations in a same-paragraph causal chain.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows avoidance, staying busy, and seeking company, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies lead to the self-blaming or mistrustful appraisals in a same-paragraph causal chain.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
